### Metabolomic profiles of the accelerometer-derived physical activity

The total volume of physical activity (TPA) was associated with 195 of 249 metabolites (78%) at a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05 (Supplementary Table S3), and 146 metabolites remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Among these 146 associations, 107 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort, including 2 apolipoproteins, 1 cholesterol, 1 cholesterol ester, 6 fatty acids, 1 fluid balance marker, 2 free cholesterols, 1 glycolysis-related metabolite, 1 inflammatory marker, 1 lipid metabolism ratio, 2 lipoprotein particle concentrations, 2 lipoprotein particle sizes, 76 lipoprotein subclasses, 3 other lipids, 3 phospholipids, and 2 triglycerides (Supplementary Table S4).

In the UKB discovery cohort, MVPA was associated with 173 of 249 metabolites (69%) at a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05, and 125 metabolites remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Among these 125 associations, 92 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort, including 65 lipoprotein subclasses, 2 apolipoproteins, 1 cholesterol, 1 cholesteryl ester, 5 fatty acids, 1 free cholesterol, 1 inflammatory marker, 1 lipid metabolite ratio, 2 lipoprotein particle concentrations, 2 lipoprotein particle sizes, 1 phospholipid, 3 other lipids, 5 total lipids, and 2 triglycerides. Light-intensity physical activity was associated with 164 of 249 metabolites (66%) at FDR < 0.05, with 90 metabolites remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Of these 90 associations, 15 (56%) were validated in the internal UKB validation cohort. Further details regarding the discovery and validation sets were provided in Supplementary Tables S4, S5 and Fig. 2(A). ## Discussion

In this prospective cohort, higher levels of accelerometer-measured MVPA and TPA showed significant inverse correlations with stroke risk, consistent with previous findings [4]. We have identified 32 TPA-related metabolites, 11 MVPA-related metabolites, and 5 LPA-related metabolites. Building on these results, we developed TPA-MetS, MVPA-MetS, and LPA-MetS to comprehensively assess how physical activity-associated metabolomic patterns mediate the physical activity-stroke association, while also elucidating individual metabolites' contributions within these signatures. Mediation analyses demonstrate that both TPA and MVPA-associated metabolomic signatures significantly attenuated stroke risk through distinct mechanisms. Single-mediator analyses further revealed that TPA primarily conferred protection via modulation of lipoprotein interactions and fatty acid metabolism, whereas MVPA specifically targeted very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) metabolic pathways.

Our results revealed the stroke-preventive potential of TPA and MVPA, along with their underlying metabolic regulatory mechanisms. Notably, the integrated metabolomic signatures demonstrated significantly better explanatory power for stroke risk than individual metabolites, highlighting the systemic advantages of metabolic network regulation.

The functional significance of these metabolomic signatures aligns with fundamental principles of metabolic regulation. Metabolites serve not merely as biochemical endpoints but as crucial regulatory molecules bridging environmental exposures and cellular physiological states [9]. Their dynamic changes reflect the organism's adaptive responses to external stimuli and form molecular connections between exposures and phenotypic outcomes [10]. The construction of metabolic signatures not only facilitates the exploration of the link between physical activity and stroke, but also reveals potential common metabolic responses of the body to physical activity [9]. However, the heterogeneity in metabolic responses among individuals exposed to the same level of physical activity should not be overlooked [28]. Metabolites identified through the development of such metabolic signatures may serve as potential biomarkers reflecting physical activity responses [29]. Monitoring these biomarkers during physical activity could help identify individuals who do not exhibit beneficial metabolic changes following appropriate levels of exercise prior to the onset of stroke, allowing for timely adjustments to prevention strategies [28].

Our findings are consistent with previous research on physical activity-induced metabolic effects, such as the Finnish Twin Cohort Study demonstrating that sustained physical activity promotes conversion of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids while reducing VLDL concentrations [16]. Given the established roles of inflammation and oxidative stress in stroke pathogenesis, our observation that both TPA and MVPA signatures include glycoprotein acetylation (an inflammatory marker) supports the hypothesis that physical activity mitigates these pathological processes through multiple pathways. This observation aligns with established mechanisms whereby physical activity promotes Nrf2 nuclear translocation and downstream activation of antioxidant gene expression [30]. The apolipoprotein B/apolipoprotein A-I (apoB/apo A-I) ratio demonstrates superior predictive value compared to traditional lipid parameters [31]. Studies have demonstrated that physical activity reduces apoB levels through decreasing visceral adipose tissue, consequently leading to a lower apoB/apo A-I ratio [32].

Different Physical activity intensity appears to induce distinct metabolic effects [9,33]. Animal studies had shown that moderate-intensity exercised activates ventromedial hypothalamic (VMH) noradrenergic neurons to enhance white adipose tissue fatty acid oxidation [34], while high-intensity could exercise modulates gut microbiota to reduce inflammatory cytokines [35]. Clinical evidence also corroborated our findings: A cross-sectional study demonstrated MVPA's (but not LPA's) important role in reducing VLDL particle concentration and size, particularly in populations with cardiovascular risk factors [36]. A case-control study reported significantly improved lipid profiles, including reduced TC, increased HDL-C, and lowered atherogenic indices, in high-intensity physical activity groups [37]. This finding is consistent with our observed MVPA-specific regulation of lipoprotein metabolism. Although we have identified LPA-associated metabolic signatures, their lack of direct association with stroke risk suggests that MVPA may offer more definitive preventive benefits. This aligns with existing evidence that regular MVPA not only reduces stroke risk but also ameliorates key risk factors like hypertension and diabetes [3,38].

Although the metabolites incorporated into the metabolomic signatures were generally consistent with previous studies [6], We systematically assessed mediation by both metabolomic signatures and its constituent metabolites, quantifying how distinct levels of physical activity confer stroke protection. Mediation analysis of metabolomic signatures components revealed that lipoprotein subclasses mediated effects for both TPA and MVPA, while omega-6 fatty acid proportions specifically mediated TPA effects. The strongest mediators were cholesteryl esters to total lipids in l-HDL, triglycerides in s-HDL, and omega-6 fatty acids to total fatty acids ratio.Prior research indicates HDL cholesterol esterification plays a vital role in reverse cholesterol transport and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prevention [39]. This explains the significant mediating effect of elevated cholesteryl ester proportion in HDL on reduced stroke risk observed in our study. In our study, TPA demonstrated an inverse correlation with small HDL triglyceride (HDL-TG) levels. Previous research has demonstrated that increased levels of small HDL-TG can impair HDL function and are correlated with metabolic disturbances, including hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, as well as cardiovascular risks like carotid plaque formation [40].

In sensitivity analyses stratified by stroke etiology, the inverse associations of both TPA- and MVPA-related metabolomic signatures with stroke risk were predominantly observed for ischemic stroke, while no significant associations were detected for hemorrhagic subtypes. This finding suggests that the protective associations of physical activity-related metabolomic features are stronger for ischemic stroke than for hemorrhagic stroke, indicating that these signatures primarily reflect pathways related to atherosclerosis and metabolic mechanisms, such as improved lipid metabolism and reduced inflammation [41,42]. In contrast, hemorrhagic stroke is more influenced by vascular fragility and hypertension-related processes [43], which are less represented in physical activity-induced metabolic alterations. Future studies integrating metabolomics, proteomics, and vascular imaging data are warranted to elucidate these subtype-specific mechanisms.

This study has several strengths. First, the large-scale cohort with high-quality metabolomics and precisely measured physical activity ensured robust findings. Second, we provided the first comprehensive metabolomic characterization of physical activity's biological mechanisms in stroke prevention, with quantitative comparison of protective effects across the volume of physical activity through mediation analyses.

However, this study has certain limitations that should be acknowledged. First, notwithstanding the prospective design, multivariable adjustments, and mediation analyses employed to bolster the robustness of our causal inference, the possibility of residual confounding cannot be entirely ruled out. These methodological strengths remain insufficient to establish causality. Future studies are warranted to confirm a causal relationship. Second, the mediation analysis employed a simplified model of potential pathways through which physical activity may influence stroke occurrence, and future studies should investigate additional mediating factors. Third, the study population was exclusively drawn from the United Kingdom; Future research should evaluate the generalizability of these findings to different populations. Fourth, although the accelerometer provides an objective measure of the volume and intensity of physical activity, it cannot distinguish the context or purpose of the movement (e.g., structured exercise versus occupational activity). Finally, the metabolic effects of physical activity exhibit notable temporal specificity. Our study did not analyze levels of physical activity in specific time windows; future research could explore how the chronobiology of physical activity (e.g., time of day) influences metabolic profiles.

## Conclusion

Our study elucidated the metabolomic mechanisms underlying the inverse association between physical activity and stroke risk. We identified distinct metabolic signatures (TPA-MetS, MVPA-MetS) reflecting levels of physical activity. Key mediators included lipoprotein subclasses and fatty acids, highlighting the role of lipid metabolism and inflammation in stroke prevention. Our findings advanced the understanding of physical activity's protective effects by linking objective activity metrics to systemic metabolic reprogramming, offering novel biomarkers for precision prevention and interventions.
